claim: Monkey S is a female Rhesus macaque, 7 years old, weighing 6.25 kg.
source: A female Rhesus macaque (monkey S; 7 years; 6.25 kg) initially showed comparable behaviour to cage mates, and successfully followed the same familiarisation and training pattern for coming out from the home enclosure into a transport box or primate chair (Mason et al., 2019).
evidence: Direct statement in the case history section providing demographic information about the subject.

claim: Monkey S initially showed comparable behaviour to cage mates.
source: A female Rhesus macaque (monkey S; 7 years; 6.25 kg) initially showed comparable behaviour to cage mates, and successfully followed the same familiarisation and training pattern for coming out from the home enclosure into a transport box or primate chair (Mason et al., 2019).
evidence: Observational data from behavioral assessment.

claim: Monkey S successfully followed the same familiarisation and training pattern for coming out from the home enclosure into a transport box or primate chair as other monkeys.
source: A female Rhesus macaque (monkey S; 7 years; 6.25 kg) initially showed comparable behaviour to cage mates, and successfully followed the same familiarisation and training pattern for coming out from the home enclosure into a transport box or primate chair (Mason et al., 2019).
evidence: Direct observation of training outcomes with citation to methods.

claim: Training in both transport box and primate chair was completed in a comparable time frame to other monkeys trained at the same time.
source: Training in both cases was completed in a comparable time frame to other monkeys trained at the same time.
evidence: Comparative training data across subjects.

claim: Task training for monkey S took place five days per week over 18 months.
source: Subsequently, task training took place five days per week over 18 months – this involved visual tasks but was intended for a decision-making study, rather than for measurement of visual performance.
evidence: Direct statement of training protocol duration and frequency.

claim: Monkey S managed to complete 10 trials in 3 min within one week of training on the 'anytouch' task.
source: Monkey S managed to complete 10 trials in 3 min within one week of training and thus progressed to the next training stage.
evidence: Specific performance metrics from training sessions.

claim: Monkey S reached 40–50 trials in the 'oneplace' task but continued with the lowest complexity of visual presentations over six weeks of training.
source: Monkey S reached 40–50 trials in increments of 10 trials, but continued with the lowest complexity of visual presentations over six weeks of training.
evidence: Training performance data showing limited progression.

claim: Monkey S completed 40–50 trials in a time window ranging between 30–91 min per session, which was particularly poor performance compared with other monkeys.
source: The 40–50 trials were completed in a time window ranging between 30–91 min per session. This was a particularly poor performance compared with other monkeys progressing through this auto-shaping programme.
evidence: Comparative performance data across subjects.

claim: Monkey S was unable to progress further from the initial stages of 'oneplace'.
source: Monkey S was unable to progress further from the initial stages of 'oneplace'.
evidence: Direct observation of training limitations.

claim: Monkey S attained 40 rewarded trials in 33 min over many weeks of training sessions in the primate chair, whereas typical performance is expected to be closer to 100 rewarded trials in 18–25 min.
source: Monkey S still worked much more slowly than other monkeys, attaining 40 rewarded trials in 33 min over many weeks of training sessions, whereas typical performance is expected to be closer to 100 rewarded trials in 18–25 min.
evidence: Comparative performance data with normative expectations.

claim: Monkey S would typically no longer respond to the task when the number of trials or the complexity of the task were increased.
source: Monkey S would typically no longer respond to the task when the number of trials or the complexity of the task were increased.
evidence: Behavioral observation during training.

claim: Monkey S was unable to learn to release the lever in response to visual stimulation.
source: Although she did well during this initial behavioural training, monkey S was unable to learn to release the lever in response to visual stimulation.
evidence: Training outcome data showing specific deficit.

claim: Monkey S typically only completed up to 10–20 trials towards the end of six months of training on the spatial search task and only when the trainer remained present in the room.
source: When monkey S was required to do a simple spatial search using the lever in response to a change in target colour on the screen, she typically only completed up to 10–20 trials towards the end of six months of training and only when the trainer remained present in the room.
evidence: Training performance data with contextual factors.

claim: While seated in the primate chair, monkey S could orient towards rewards and objects when held up in front of her and when moved around in her visual field.
source: During this time, rudimentary checks determined that, while seated in the primate chair, monkey S could orient towards rewards and objects when held up in front of her and when moved around in her visual field.
evidence: Direct behavioral observation of visual orienting ability.

claim: Monkey S completed up to 40 trials for banana pellets after 6 weeks of training, but still required 41–103 mins to complete a session, making between 23–51 errors.
source: She completed up to 40 trials for banana pellets after 6 weeks of training, but still required 41–103 mins to complete a session, making between 23–51 errors.
evidence: Quantitative training performance data.

claim: Behavioural assessment in the home enclosure by a clinical neurologist and two neuroscientists showed no qualitatively different patterns of locomotion and visual orienting towards other monkeys and people in the room for monkey S.
source: In spite of the inability of S to perform these tested psychophysical tasks, behavioural assessment in the home enclosure by a clinical neurologist and two neuroscientists showed no qualitatively different patterns of locomotion and visual orienting towards other monkeys and people in the room.
evidence: Expert clinical assessment of behavior.

claim: There was some indication that patterns of eye fixation might be atypical in monkey S, but no quantitative assessment was undertaken.
source: There was some indication that patterns of eye fixation might be atypical, but no quantitative assessment was undertaken.
evidence: Qualitative observation without quantitative measurement.

claim: When monkey S was offered treats, she would start repeatedly running past the treat and pick it up with a sideways reach while running - rather than coming forwards, fixating the treat and reaching for it in a more controlled way.
source: However, when monkey S was offered treats, she would start repeatedly running past the treat and pick it up with a sideways reach while running - rather than coming forwards, fixating the treat and reaching for it in a more controlled way.
evidence: Behavioral observation of atypical reaching behavior.

claim: Structural MRI revealed an almost complete loss of primary visual cortex (V1) in monkey S.
source: Structural MRI revealed an almost complete loss of primary visual cortex (V1) (Figure 1, top), consistent with presumptive bilateral visual field loss (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: MRI imaging data showing anatomical lesion.

claim: The lesion in monkey S is consistent with presumptive bilateral visual field loss.
source: Structural MRI revealed an almost complete loss of primary visual cortex (V1) (Figure 1, top), consistent with presumptive bilateral visual field loss (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Inference from anatomical lesion location to functional deficit.

claim: Clinical assessment of the MRI scans and records suggested no injury or history that could explain the lesion in monkey S and that this was probably a congenital or perinatal condition.
source: Clinical assessment of the MRI scans and records suggested no injury or history that could explain this lesion and that this was probably a congenital or perinatal condition.
evidence: Clinical interpretation of imaging and medical history.

claim: The LGN and pulvinar are visible in parasagittal, coronal, and horizontal sections in monkey S.
source: LGN (white arrow) and pulvinar (posterior and dorsal to LGN) are shown in parasagittal section (with high magnification inset) as well as in the coronal and horizontal sections.
evidence: Direct observation from MRI images.

claim: Based on established neurophysiological maps of V1 retinotopy, bilateral visual field loss is expected for the central 10° as well as for more peripheral parts, potentially around 15°−20° eccentricity in monkey S.
source: Based on established neurophysiological maps of V1 retinotopy in relation to the cortical folding pattern and approximate slice position (their Figure 11, Van Essen et al., 1984), we estimated the visual field loss of monkey S. The visual map is shown on post mortem T2*-weighted images – deformations of the occipital cortical surface were post mortem. Given the extent of the loss of white matter directly underneath V1, we expect bilateral visual field loss, for the central 10° as well as for more peripheral parts, potentially around 15°−20° eccentricity.
evidence: Inference based on established retinotopic maps and anatomical lesion extent.

claim: In humans with lesions of V1 resulting in hemianopia, the LGN is often reduced in size due to retrograde degeneration.
source: In humans with lesions of V1, which result in hemianopia, the LGN is often reduced in size, due to retrograde degeneration (Miki et al., 2005; Bridge et al., 2011).
evidence: Cited findings from human studies.

claim: A similar result of LGN size reduction has been found in the adult marmoset with V1 lesions.
source: A similar result has also been found in the adult marmoset (Atapour et al., 2017).
evidence: Cited findings from marmoset studies.

claim: There was no obvious reduction in size of the LGN in monkey S from inspection of the images.
source: When we investigated the structure of the LGN in monkey S and four female control Rhesus macaques of a similar age with intact visual systems, there was no obvious reduction in size of the structure from inspection of the images (Figure 1).
evidence: Visual inspection of MRI images comparing subject to controls.

claim: The volume of the LGN in the control monkeys was measured at 50.0 mm3 ± 4.7 mm3 and 51.5 mm3 ± 5.1 mm3 (mean ± SD) for the left and right hemispheres.
source: The volume of the LGN in the control monkeys was measured at 50.0 mm3 ± 4.7 mm3 and 51.5 mm3 ± 5.1 mm3 (mean ± SD) for the left and right hemispheres.
evidence: Quantitative volumetric measurements from control subjects.

claim: In monkey S, the LGN volumes were 47.0 mm3 and 48.5 mm3 for left and right hemispheres respectively.
source: In monkey S, the comparable values were 47.0 mm3 and 48.5 mm3 respectively.
evidence: Quantitative volumetric measurements from monkey S.

claim: The LGN structure in monkey S seems not to have been affected by retrograde degeneration.
source: Thus, the structure seems not to have been affected by retrograde degeneration.
evidence: Inference from volumetric comparison showing no reduction.

claim: The superior colliculus (SC) was comparable in size in monkey S (left = 30.0 mm3; right = 31.6 mm3) and control monkeys (left = 31.0 mm3 ± 1.9 mm3 and right = 30.5 mm3 ± 3.3 mm3).
source: Similarly, the superior colliculus (SC) was also comparable in size in monkey S (left = 30.0 mm3; right = 31.6 mm3) and control monkeys (left = 31.0 mm3 ± 1.9 mm3 and right = 30.5 mm3 ± 3.3 mm3) (mean ± SD).
evidence: Quantitative volumetric comparison between subject and controls.

claim: The pulvinar was of a similar size in monkey S (left = 40.2 mm3; right = 41.9 mm3) and control monkeys (left = 37.7 mm3 ± 4.4 mm3 and right = 35.9 mm3±3.2 mm3).
source: Finally, the pulvinar was also of a similar size in monkey S (left = 40.2 mm3; right = 41.9 mm3) and control monkeys (left = 37.7 mm3 ± 4.4 mm3 and right = 35.9 mm3±3.2 mm3) (mean ± SD).
evidence: Quantitative volumetric comparison between subject and controls.

claim: The stripe of Gennari is visible in both monkey S and the control monkey in post mortem T2*-weighted images.
source: A post mortem T2*-weighted structural scan at high field (7T) revealed the stripe of Gennari in V1 (white arrows for example sites) of both monkey S and a control monkey (M131), although the position relative to the cortical surface within the cortical ribbon appeared to differ.
evidence: Direct observation from high-resolution post mortem imaging.

claim: The stripe of Gennari is closer to the pial surface in monkey S, rather than in the middle of the cortical ribbon as seen in the control monkey.
source: However, the stripe is closer to the pial surface in monkey S, rather than in the middle of the cortical ribbon, as seen in the control monkey.
evidence: Comparative observation from imaging data.

claim: The superficial layers of V1 are particularly reduced as a consequence of the extensive lesion in monkey S.
source: This could suggest that the superficial layers are particularly reduced as a consequence of the extensive lesion.
evidence: Inference from the position of the stripe of Gennari.

claim: Monkey S has substantially thinner V1 cortex around the lesion compared to the control monkey.
source: Measurement of cortical thickness in V1 in both monkeys indicated that monkey S has substantially thinner cortex around the lesion.
evidence: Quantitative measurement of cortical thickness.

claim: The V1 grey matter in monkey S was reduced in thickness to 0.9–1.3 mm around the enlarged ventricles (1.4–1.8 mm in the control).
source: The V1 grey matter in monkey S was reduced in thickness to 0.9–1.3 mm around the enlarged ventricles (1.4–1.8 mm in the control).
evidence: Quantitative thickness measurements from imaging.

claim: Extrastriate visual area V5/MT appeared to have a thickness of about 2 mm in monkey S, which is comparable to the control monkey.
source: By contrast, extrastriate visual area V5/MT appeared to have a thickness of about 2 mm, which is comparable to the control monkey.
evidence: Comparative thickness measurement.

claim: The grey matter at the location for V5/MT appeared intact with a typical thickness of 1.9–2.0 mm in monkey S.
source: By contrast, the grey matter at the location for V5/MT appeared intact with a typical thickness of 1.9–2.0 mm.
evidence: Quantitative measurement from imaging.

claim: T1w/T2w structural MRI images provide a qualitative signal indicative of myelination within the cortical ribbon in vivo.
source: T1w/T2w structural MRI images provide a qualitative signal indicative of myelination within the cortical ribbon in vivo (Glasser and Van Essen, 2011; Large et al., 2016).
evidence: Cited methodological principle.

claim: Myelin-weighted images show a distinct band indicative of dense myelination in the lower layers of extrastriate cortical area V5/MT on the posterior bank of the dorsal superior temporal sulcus (STS) in monkey S, similar in location and extent to the four control monkeys.
source: These myelin-weighted images show a distinct band indicative of dense myelination in the lower layers of extrastriate cortical area V5/MT on the posterior bank of the dorsal superior temporal sulcus (STS), but not in adjacent cortical areas. This band is similar in location and extent to the four control monkeys.
evidence: Comparative analysis of myelin-weighted imaging.

claim: The mean surface area of the region of distinct myelination in dorsal STS (likely to comprise V5/MT and MST) was measured as 86.9 mm2 (left hemisphere) and 78.8 mm2 (right hemisphere) in monkey S.
source: We measured the mean surface area of this region of distinct myelination (top third of image intensity values) in dorsal STS, likely to comprise V5/MT and MST, as 86.9 mm2 (left hemisphere) and 78.8 mm2.
evidence: Quantitative measurement from myelin-weighted images.

claim: The measured surface area of V5/MT and MST in monkey S is in the range of published data of 82.4 mm2 (SD = ±8.9; n = 10 hemispheres) obtained by the same method.
source: This is in the range of published data of 82.4 mm2 (SD = ±8.9; n = 10 hemispheres) obtained by the same method (Large et al., 2016).
evidence: Comparison with published normative data.

claim: Eight scanning sessions were conducted in seven Rhesus macaque monkeys.
source: We conducted eight scanning sessions in seven Rhesus macaque monkeys.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental design.

claim: Analyses were restricted to monkeys that had significant BOLD activation in the LGN (z > 2.3) to the checkerboard stimulus.
source: We then restricted all further analyses to those monkeys that had significant BOLD activation in the LGN (z > 2.3) to this stimulus (see Materials and methods and Figure 4; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Methodological criterion for inclusion in analysis.

claim: One scanning session from each of four monkeys fulfilled the criterion of significant LGN activation, including the first of two separate scanning sessions with monkey S.
source: One scanning session from each of four monkeys fulfilled this criterion, including the first of two separate scanning sessions with monkey S.
evidence: Results of applying inclusion criteria.

claim: LGN was significantly activated in all monkeys by flickering checkerboards (z > 2.3).
source: LGN was significantly activated in all monkeys by flickering checkerboards (z > 2.3).
evidence: fMRI activation data from visual stimulation.

claim: Cortical activation to checkerboards is less consistent across the control monkeys and not really evident in monkey S.
source: Cortical activation is less consistent across the control monkeys and not really evident in monkey S.
evidence: Comparative analysis of fMRI activation patterns.

claim: The pulvinar was not consistently activated by the checkerboard stimulus.
source: The parasagittal sections show that the pulvinar was not consistently activated by this stimulus.
evidence: fMRI activation data showing lack of consistent response.

claim: The strong activation evident in the LGN of monkey S is consistent with the intact structure shown in Figure 1, and suggests that information from the retina can reach the brain.
source: The strong activation evident in the LGN of monkey S, is consistent with the intact structure shown in Figure 1, and suggests that information from the retina can reach the brain.
evidence: Inference from functional activation and structural integrity.

claim: The control monkeys showed similar activation in the LGN in response to the checkerboard stimulus.
source: The control monkeys included in these analyses showed similar activation in the LGN in response to this stimulus.
evidence: Comparative fMRI activation data.

claim: There was less activation evident in visual cortical regions in response to checkerboards, especially in the primary visual cortex of monkey S.
source: In contrast to the strong activation in the LGN, there was less activation evident in visual cortical regions, especially in the primary visual cortex of monkey S (see Figure 4—figure supplement 2 for a complete series of sections).
evidence: fMRI activation data showing reduced cortical response.

claim: Even in the control monkeys there was considerable variability in the location and extent of cortical BOLD activation to checkerboards.
source: Even in the control monkeys there was considerable variability in the location and extent of cortical BOLD activation.
evidence: Observation of variability in fMRI data across subjects.

claim: The checkerboard stimulus is expected to activate V1.
source: The checkerboard stimulus is expected to activate V1, but even in some control animals where V1 is intact, the activation was not extensive.
evidence: Based on known properties of visual stimuli and V1 function.

claim: Some of the variability in cortical activation may be due to effects of anaesthesia on visual responses.
source: Some of this variability may be due to effects of anaesthesia on visual responses (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1; see Discussion).
evidence: Speculation about confounding factors affecting results.

claim: The level of activation to moving dots was lower in all animals, including monkey S, compared to checkerboards.
source: The responses to moving dots compared to stationary dots are shown in Figure 5. The level of activation to this type of stimulation was lower in all animals, including monkey S.
evidence: Comparative fMRI activation data across stimulus types.

claim: Control monkey M901 showed very little activation to the moving dots in any brain region, in contrast to the strong activation evident in the LGN to flickering checkerboards.
source: Control monkey M901 showed very little activation to the moving dots in any brain region, in contrast to the strong activation evident in the LGN to flickering checkerboards.
evidence: Individual subject fMRI data showing stimulus-specific response pattern.

claim: Monkey S showed some LGN activation on the left side of the brain and in the pulvinar situated posterior to the LGN in response to moving dots.
source: Monkey S showed some LGN activation on the left side of the brain and in the pulvinar situated posterior to the LGN.
evidence: fMRI activation data for moving dot stimulus.

claim: Cortical activation to moving dots was sparsely distributed around the brain, with some activation within the dorsal part of the Superior Temporal Sulcus (STS) near area V5/MT in monkey S and in control monkeys M142 and M902.
source: Cortical activation was sparsely distributed around the brain, with some activation within the dorsal part of the Superior Temporal Sulcus (STS) near area V5/MT in monkey S (see Figure 5—figure supplement 1) and in control monkeys M142 and M902.
evidence: fMRI activation data showing spatial distribution of responses.

claim: Activation in LGN is greatest to the flickering checkerboard across all animals, including monkey S.
source: The activation levels in Figure 6 support the observation that the activity in LGN is greatest to the checkerboards across all animals, including monkey S.
evidence: Quantitative comparison of fMRI activation levels.

claim: For control monkeys, V1 activation tended to be lower than for the LGN, with a median ratio of V1:LGN of 0.83 (range 0.2–0.92).
source: For control monkeys, V1 activation tended to be lower than for the LGN, with a median ratio of V1:LGN of 0.83 (range 0.2–0.92), but this was 0 for monkey S as she showed no V1 activation.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of relative activation levels.

claim: The V1:LGN activation ratio was 0 for monkey S as she showed no V1 activation.
source: For control monkeys, V1 activation tended to be lower than for the LGN, with a median ratio of V1:LGN of 0.83 (range 0.2–0.92), but this was 0 for monkey S as she showed no V1 activation.
evidence: Quantitative analysis showing absence of V1 activation.

claim: Monkey S did not show significant activation in anatomically defined area V5/MT to either checkerboard or moving dot stimulus.
source: Furthermore, monkey S did not show significant activation in anatomically defined area V5/MT to either stimulus but did in the pulvinar, though only in response to the moving dots.
evidence: fMRI activation data from region of interest analysis.

claim: Monkey S showed significant activation in the pulvinar, though only in response to the moving dots.
source: Furthermore, monkey S did not show significant activation in anatomically defined area V5/MT to either stimulus but did in the pulvinar, though only in response to the moving dots.
evidence: fMRI activation data showing stimulus-specific response.

claim: The only other monkey with activation in the pulvinar to the moving dots (M902) showed similar activation to the checkerboard stimulus, a pattern not seen in monkey S.
source: The only other monkey with activation in the pulvinar to the moving dots (M902) showed similar activation to the checkerboard stimulus, a pattern not seen in monkey S.
evidence: Comparative analysis of activation patterns across subjects.

claim: The pathways most often proposed to underlie blindsight in human patients with hemianopia include the visual motion complex hMT+.
source: The pathways most often proposed to underlie blindsight in human patients with hemianopia include the visual motion complex hMT+ (thought to comprise visual areas V5/MT and MST) and this region often shows significant activation in response to moving stimuli, similar to the stimulus used here (Ajina et al., 2015a; Ajina and Bridge, 2016), and to contrast defined stimuli (Ajina et al., 2015c).
evidence: Cited findings from human blindsight literature.

claim: hMT+ often shows significant activation in response to moving stimuli in human patients with hemianopia.
source: The pathways most often proposed to underlie blindsight in human patients with hemianopia include the visual motion complex hMT+ (thought to comprise visual areas V5/MT and MST) and this region often shows significant activation in response to moving stimuli, similar to the stimulus used here (Ajina et al., 2015a; Ajina and Bridge, 2016), and to contrast defined stimuli (Ajina et al., 2015c).
evidence: Cited findings from human studies.

claim: There were a number of regions within the sulcus showing BOLD activation (z > 2.3) to the moving dot stimulus in monkey S, including in area MST on the anterior bank and area FST at the bottom of the sulcus, but mainly outside V5/MT.
source: While there was no spatially extensive region of activation, there were a number of regions within the sulcus showing BOLD activation (z > 2.3) to the moving dot stimulus, including in area MST on the anterior bank and area FST at the bottom of the sulcus, but mainly outside V5/MT.
evidence: Detailed spatial analysis of fMRI activation.

claim: It is conceivable that the heavily enlarged, fluid-filled ventricles within the visual cortex that formed the lesion could have differentially affected the pattern of action of anaesthesia in monkey S.
source: For instance, it is conceivable that the heavily enlarged, fluid-filled ventricles within the visual cortex that formed the lesion could have differentially affected the pattern of action of anaesthesia in monkey S.
evidence: Speculation about potential confounding factor.

claim: Regions of the cortex with a pattern of BOLD activation significantly correlated to the time-series signal extracted from V5/MT on the right side of the brain were identified when the monkey was shown the moving dot stimulus.
source: Figure 8 shows the regions of the cortex with a pattern of BOLD activation that was significantly correlated to the time-series signal extracted from V5/MT on the right side of the brain when the monkey was shown the moving dot stimulus.
evidence: Results of functional connectivity analysis.

claim: The pattern of activation from V5/MT connectivity analysis was bilateral, which would be expected since both sides of the brain received the same visual stimulation.
source: The nature of the analysis ensured that V5/MT in the right hemisphere must have a significant correlation, but clearly the two hemispheres had similar connectivity as the pattern of activation we found was bilateral. This would be expected since both sides of the brain received the same visual stimulation.
evidence: Inference from experimental design and results.

claim: A large swathe of dorsal extrastriate cortex and parietal areas showed significant correlation with V5/MT, both in the control monkeys and in monkey S.
source: In addition to the STS, a large swathe of dorsal extrastriate cortex and parietal areas showed significant correlation, both in the control monkeys and in monkey S.
evidence: Results of functional connectivity analysis.

claim: The network connected to V5/MT included the Frontal Eye Fields (FEF) in monkey S and all control monkeys.
source: Finally, the network connected to V5/MT included the Frontal Eye Fields (FEF) in monkey S and all control monkeys.
evidence: Results of functional connectivity analysis.

claim: The network of cortical regions showing significant correlation with V5/MT is consistent across all animals, including monkey S.
source: The network of cortical regions showing significant correlation is consistent across all animals, including monkey S, and consists predominantly of dorsal occipital and parietal regions as well as area FEF (black arrows).
evidence: Comparative analysis of functional connectivity patterns.

claim: Despite individual differences in the level of cortical activation, a bilateral pattern of dorsal but not ventral visual activation emerged from the connectivity analysis.
source: Despite individual differences in the level of cortical activation, a bilateral pattern of dorsal but not ventral visual activation emerged.
evidence: Summary of functional connectivity results.

claim: Neither LGN nor pulvinar as seeds produced a consistent pattern of connectivity with any cortical structures either in the control monkeys or monkey S.
source: This connectivity analysis was also performed using the LGN and the pulvinar as a seed. Neither of these seeds produced a consistent pattern of connectivity with any cortical structures either in the control monkeys or monkey S.
evidence: Results of functional connectivity analysis with different seed regions.

claim: The structural data indicated that both V5/MT and LGN were intact in monkey S.
source: The structural data indicated that both V5/MT and LGN were intact in monkey S, and fMRI activation data suggested that LGN and pulvinar were activated by a flickering checkerboard and moving dots respectively.
evidence: Summary of structural and functional imaging findings.

claim: fMRI activation data suggested that LGN and pulvinar were activated by a flickering checkerboard and moving dots respectively in monkey S.
source: The structural data indicated that both V5/MT and LGN were intact in monkey S, and fMRI activation data suggested that LGN and pulvinar were activated by a flickering checkerboard and moving dots respectively.
evidence: Summary of functional imaging findings.

claim: Extrastriate visual area V5/MT appeared to have a similar functional connectivity profile to this area as observed in control monkeys.
source: Furthermore, extrastriate visual area V5/MT appeared to have a similar functional connectivity profile to this area as observed in control monkeys.
evidence: Comparative analysis of functional connectivity.

claim: The six control monkeys showed reasonably consistent tracts between pulvinar and V5/MT and between LGN and V5/MT.
source: The six control monkeys showed reasonably consistent tracts with pulvinar<->V5/MT tract generally running superior to the LGN<->V5/MT tract.
evidence: Results of probabilistic tractography in control subjects.

claim: The pulvinar<->V5/MT tract generally runs superior to the LGN<->V5/MT tract in control monkeys.
source: The six control monkeys showed reasonably consistent tracts with pulvinar<->V5/MT tract generally running superior to the LGN<->V5/MT tract.
evidence: Spatial relationship observed in tractography data.

claim: Monkey S showed tracts between LGN/pulvinar and V5/MT, but the location and extent of the lesion meant that the actual route followed was different and the tracts seemed to be less direct as they appeared to project around the lesion.
source: Monkey S also showed tracts between these structures, but the location and extent of the lesion meant that the actual route followed was different and the tracts seemed to be less direct as they appeared to project around the lesion.
evidence: Tractography results showing altered pathway routing.

claim: The microstructure of the tracts in monkey S was most likely intact based on fractional anisotropy (FA) values.
source: These metrics are shown in Figure 10, and indicate that the microstructure of the tracts in monkey S was most likely intact.
evidence: Quantitative diffusion imaging metrics.

claim: The number of tracts that could be identified between V5/MT and either LGN or pulvinar was very low in monkey S, with the percentage of tracts reaching target ranging between 0.01–0.03% in all cases.
source: But the number of tracts that could be identified between V5/MT and either LGN or pulvinar was very low, with the percentage of tracts reaching target ranging between 0.01–0.03% in all cases for monkey S.
evidence: Quantitative tractography metrics.

claim: The percentage of tracts reaching target in monkey S was at least an order of magnitude lower compared to control monkeys.
source: Compared to control monkeys, this was at least an order of magnitude lower.
evidence: Quantitative comparison of tractography metrics.

claim: The functional anisotropy values for the tracts in monkey S were comparable to the control values for both LGN-V5/MT and pulvinar-V5/MT pathways.
source: By contrast, the functional anisotropy values for the tracts in monkey S were comparable to the control values for both pathways. This suggests that the white matter microstructure within the tracts between V5/MT and each target structure was intact.
evidence: Quantitative comparison of diffusion metrics.

claim: The white matter microstructure within the tracts between V5/MT and each target structure was intact in monkey S.
source: By contrast, the functional anisotropy values for the tracts in monkey S were comparable to the control values for both pathways. This suggests that the white matter microstructure within the tracts between V5/MT and each target structure was intact.
evidence: Inference from comparable FA values.

claim: Given the significantly weakened tract between V5/MT and subcortical nuclei indicated by the diffusion imaging, there is little evidence to suggest that a strengthening of these connections underlies whatever residual vision was present in monkey S.
source: Given the significantly weakened tract between V5/MT and subcortical nuclei indicated by the diffusion imaging, there is little evidence to suggest that a strengthening of these connections underlies whatever residual vision was present in monkey S.
evidence: Inference from tractography results regarding mechanism of residual vision.

claim: Residual vision can manifest in the ability to determine information from faces, as shown in patient TN.
source: Residual vision can manifest in several different ways, including the ability to determine information from faces, as shown in patient TN (Burra et al., 2013), a function that has been suggested to survive loss of V1.
evidence: Cited case study from human patient literature.

claim: Clearly defined clusters of activation for the anterior (likely AF) and middle (likely MF) face patches located in the fundus of ventral STS were found in response to face stimuli in monkey S.
source: When we compared the BOLD response to all face stimuli compared to a mid-grey background (similar to the localizer used by Liu et al., 2015), we found clearly defined clusters of activation for the two most commonly identified temporal lobe face patches in the Rhesus macaque: the anterior (likely AF, Tsao et al. (2008)) and middle (likely MF, Tsao et al. (2008)) face patch located in the fundus of ventral STS (Figure 11).
evidence: fMRI activation data in response to face stimuli.

claim: One control monkey showed only the anterior face patch in response to face stimuli.
source: One control showed only the anterior face patch.
evidence: Individual subject fMRI data.

claim: The locations of the face patches in monkey S are as previously described in macaques.
source: While the locations of these areas are as previously described in macaques (Tsao et al., 2003; Pinsk et al., 2005; Tsao et al., 2008; Bell et al., 2009), we did not check the contrast against scrambled faces.
evidence: Comparison with published literature on face patch locations.

claim: No specific differences in activation between threatening and neutral facial expressions were observed in the STS, consistent with previous studies.
source: We did not observe any specific differences in activation between threatening and neutral facial expressions in the STS, consistent with previous studies (Hoffman et al., 2007; Hadj-Bouziane et al., 2008).
evidence: Comparison of activation patterns with cited literature.

claim: Children with cortical visual impairment (CVI) can easily be misdiagnosed and their behaviour can manifest as a variety of other conditions, including learning disability, without careful investigation.
source: There are several parallels in behaviour between children with cortical visual impairment (CVI) and this monkey. Children with CVI can easily be misdiagnosed and their behaviour can manifest as a variety of other conditions, including learning disability, without careful investigation (reviewed in Chokron and Dutton, 2016).
evidence: Cited review of clinical literature on CVI.

claim: Without access to imaging it would not have been possible to determine the loss of tissue in the occipital lobes in monkey S.
source: Without access to imaging it would not have been possible to determine the loss of tissue in the occipital lobes in this animal.
evidence: Inference about the necessity of imaging for diagnosis.

claim: The majority of literature relating to residual visual ability following damage to V1 describes adult-onset, unilateral damage due to stroke or trauma.
source: The majority of literature relating to residual visual ability following damage to V1 describes adult-onset, unilateral damage due to stroke or trauma (e.g. Cowey, 2010).
evidence: Summary of literature with citation.

claim: In cases of adult-onset V1 damage, the comparison between the intact and damaged hemispheres appears to show that the LGN and optic tracts are atrophied.
source: In these cases, the comparison between the intact and damaged hemispheres appears to show that the LGN and optic tracts are atrophied (Bridge et al., 2011).
evidence: Cited findings from human studies.

claim: Even when the damage to occipital cortex is congenital, there is reduction of optic tract size in the affected hemisphere.
source: There are far fewer cases of peri-natal damage, but Millington et al. (2014) showed that even when the damage to occipital cortex is congenital, there is reduction of optic tract size in the affected hemisphere, implying a reduction in LGN size.
evidence: Cited findings from congenital damage cases.

claim: A recent imaging study of a patient with bilateral occipital damage suggested atrophy of the LGN bilaterally.
source: A recent imaging study of a patient with bilateral occipital damage suggested atrophy of the LGN bilaterally (Arcaro et al., 2018).
evidence: Cited case study.

claim: Giaschi et al. (2003) described a young man with bilateral damage to the occipital cortex suffered at birth in whom hMT+ appeared to be structurally normal but did not show evidence of activation to visual stimulation.
source: Giaschi et al. (2003) described a young man with bilateral damage to the occipital cortex suffered at birth. hMT+ in that case also appeared to be structurally normal, but did not show evidence of activation to visual stimulation.
evidence: Cited case study.

claim: Combined lesion and silencing studies in macaques reinforce the requirement for an intact LGN to support remaining visual function after V1 lesions.
source: Combined lesion and silencing studies in macaques reinforce the requirement for an intact LGN to support remaining visual function after V1 lesions (Schmid et al., 2010).
evidence: Cited experimental findings from macaque studies.

claim: Preservation of structure and function of the LGN after a visual cortical lesion might depend on age at the time of lesion as well as the extent of the lesion, as studies in marmosets suggest.
source: Preservation of structure and function of the LGN after a visual cortical lesion might depend on age at the time of lesion as well as the extent of the lesion, as studies in marmosets suggest (Atapour et al., 2017; Yu et al., 2018; Hendrickson et al., 2015).
evidence: Inference from cited marmoset studies.

claim: The preservation of LGN structure in monkey S would be consistent with a very early loss of V1, possibly in utero.
source: This would be consistent with a very early loss of V1, possibly in utero, for monkey S.
evidence: Inference from structural findings and cited literature.

claim: The increased resolution of the structural scanning and consistent location of V5/MT in the macaque allowed the myelination of this area to be identified in vivo.
source: The increased resolution of the structural scanning and consistent location of V5/MT in the macaque (Zeki, 1974; Van Essen et al., 1981) allowed the myelination of this area to be identified in vivo.
evidence: Methodological capability with cited anatomical references.

claim: The variability of hMT+ location in humans makes analysis of the myelin more challenging, and thus limits opportunities to compare across the two species.
source: Conversely, the variability of hMT+ location in humans (Large et al., 2016) makes analysis of the myelin more challenging, and thus limits our opportunities to compare across the two species.
evidence: Cited finding about human anatomy and its implications.

claim: Previous work in adult-acquired hemianopia in humans has indicated that tracts between LGN and hMT+ are similar in microstructure to sighted tracts in those showing some form of residual vision.
source: Previous work in adult-acquired hemianopia in humans has indicated that tracts between LGN and hMT+ are similar in microstructure to sighted tracts in those showing some form of residual vision (Bridge et al., 2008; Ajina et al., 2015b).
evidence: Cited findings from human studies.

claim: Monkey S had very large bilateral lesions that may have caused greater disruption to the normal pattern of white matter connectivity.
source: However, monkey S had very large bilateral lesions that may have caused greater disruption to the normal pattern of white matter connectivity.
evidence: Inference from lesion characteristics.

claim: The microstructure of the tracts between V5/MT and subcortical structures appeared to be close to control values in monkey S, as was also the case in previous human studies.
source: Nonetheless, the microstructure of these tracts appeared to be close to control values, as was also the case in previous human studies, so the reduction in size could reflect a reduction in feedback connections into the LGN rather than a change in feedforward connectivity into cortex.
evidence: Comparison with human studies and inference about connectivity.

claim: The reduction in tract size in monkey S could reflect a reduction in feedback connections into the LGN rather than a change in feedforward connectivity into cortex.
source: Nonetheless, the microstructure of these tracts appeared to be close to control values, as was also the case in previous human studies, so the reduction in size could reflect a reduction in feedback connections into the LGN rather than a change in feedforward connectivity into cortex.
evidence: Inference from tractography findings.

claim: Performing BOLD fMRI in anaesthetised macaques is challenging even when the monkey has a healthy visual system.
source: Performing BOLD fMRI in anaesthetised macaques is challenging even when the monkey has a healthy visual system; this is evident in the variability in the amount of cortical activation in the control monkeys.
evidence: Observation of methodological challenges and data variability.

claim: The level of BOLD activation is affected by general anaesthesia parameters such as type and depth.
source: The level of BOLD activation is affected by general anaesthesia parameters such as type and depth (Hutchison et al., 2014; Vincent et al., 2007), although previous results do not explain the potential differences in dorsal and temporal visual activations we see.
evidence: Cited findings about effects of anesthesia on fMRI.

claim: Isoflurane anaesthetic agent preserves some visual cortical activation, at least at low doses.
source: We used isoflurane anaesthetic agent, under which it is known that some visual cortical activation is preserved, at least at low doses (Logothetis et al., 1999; Vincent et al., 2007; Goense and Logothetis, 2008).
evidence: Cited findings about isoflurane effects on visual responses.

claim: Some of the variability in cortical activity, specifically for area V5/MT, could be due to effects of the anaesthetics which vary at shorter time scales within a fMRI session.
source: However, we cannot exclude the possibility that some of the variability in cortical activity, specifically for area V5/MT, is due to effects of the anaesthetics which vary at shorter time scales within a fMRI session.
evidence: Speculation about potential confounding factors.

claim: Some variability in cortical activation and functional connectivity as measured with fMRI could be linked to inter-individual differences in the morphology of sulcal patterns.
source: It has also been suggested that some variability in cortical activation and functional connectivity as measured with fMRI could be linked to inter-individual differences in the morphology of sulcal patterns (Lopez-Persem et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2019).
evidence: Cited findings about anatomical variability effects.

claim: Some of the small patches of activations around dorsal and ventral STS in monkey S could be spurious signal fluctuations.
source: In the same context, some of the small patches of activations that we see around dorsal and ventral STS in monkey S could be spurious signal fluctuations.
evidence: Speculation about data interpretation.

claim: A further challenge in monkey S is that the damage is bilateral, whereas in much of the previous work in humans, the sighted hemisphere has been used as a control area.
source: A further challenge in monkey S is that the damage is bilateral. In much of the previous work in humans, the sighted hemisphere has been used as a control area, therefore controlling for any global variation in activation levels.
evidence: Methodological limitation compared to human studies.

claim: The most evident activation is in the LGN in response to checkerboard stimulation, which is equivalent to that seen in controls and suggests the visual pathway prior to V1 is intact.
source: The most evident activation is clearly in the LGN in response to checkerboard stimulation, which is equivalent to that seen in controls and suggests the visual pathway prior to V1 is intact.
evidence: Summary of fMRI findings with inference about pathway integrity.

claim: The activation level in the LGN to moving dots was considerably lower than to checkerboards, which would be predicted from the properties of LGN cells.
source: The activation level to moving dots was considerably lower, but that would be predicted from the properties of LGN cells.
evidence: Observation consistent with known neurophysiology.

claim: The activation pattern in the pulvinar to moving dots for monkey S appeared to be as great as in the best control subject, which is consistent with an increased role for this structure due to the perinatal nature of the lesion.
source: By contrast, the activation pattern in the pulvinar to moving dots for monkey S appeared to be as great as in the best control subject, which is consistent with an increased role for this structure due to the perinatal nature of the lesion (Warner et al., 2015).
evidence: Comparative data with inference based on cited literature.

claim: Moving dot stimuli in the healthy and hemianopic human brain consistently lead to activation of hMT+, even when damage is bilateral.
source: Moving dot stimuli in the healthy and hemianopic human brain consistently lead to activation of hMT+, even when damage is bilateral (Arcaro et al., 2018; Bridge et al., 2010).
evidence: Cited findings from human studies.

claim: The lack of consistent activation in V5/MT in monkey S and some controls suggests a suppressive effect of the anaesthetic, which was most evident with larger doses of the volatile anaesthetic.
source: Thus, the lack of consistent activation in V5/MT in monkey S and some controls suggests a suppressive effect of the anaesthetic, which was most evident with larger doses of the volatile anaesthetic.
evidence: Inference from observed variability and anesthesia levels.

claim: Drifting eye movements and inappropriate ocular accommodation under anaesthesia could have affected the functional activation measured.
source: Also, drifting eye movements and inappropriate ocular accommodation under anaesthesia could have affected the functional activation we measured.
evidence: Speculation about potential confounding factors.

claim: For visual motion stimuli, foci of activation were seen in the region of V5/MT in dorsal STS of both hemispheres in monkey S, suggesting any activation may be sub-threshold and difficult to detect with BOLD.
source: Nevertheless, for visual motion stimuli we saw in monkey S foci of activation in the region of V5/MT in dorsal STS of both hemispheres, suggesting any activation may be sub-threshold and difficult to detect with BOLD.
evidence: Observation with inference about detection limitations.

claim: The inter-cortical activity in the macaque visual brain was not affected by the loss of V1, as suggested by the similar functional network of V5/MT in monkey S and controls.
source: This was very similar in monkey S and the control monkeys, suggesting that this inter-cortical activity in the macaque visual brain was not affected by the loss of V1.
evidence: Inference from functional connectivity analysis.

claim: None of the monkeys included LGN in the functional network connected to V5/MT, perhaps reflecting the weak anatomical connectivity between these areas in typical animals.
source: Interestingly, none of the monkeys included LGN in this functional network, perhaps reflecting the weak anatomical connectivity between these areas in typical animals (Sincich et al., 2004).
evidence: Observation with inference based on cited anatomical data.

claim: FEF was included in the functional network connected to V5/MT for all monkeys, as would be predicted from knowledge of the V5/MT connectivity.
source: For all monkeys, FEF was included in the functional network, as would be predicted from a knowledge of the V5/MT connectivity (Schall et al., 1995).
evidence: Observation consistent with cited anatomical knowledge.

claim: The activation of two face patches along the STS in monkey S suggests other intact subcortical inputs to temporal visual cortex from pulvinar, claustrum, and amygdala supporting these activations.
source: Surprisingly, we also found activation of two of the most pertinent face patches along the STS in monkey S – in the context of little other consistent activations. Without the comparison to scrambled faces, this result needs further scrutiny. However, if confirmed, this result would suggest other intact subcortical inputs in this monkey to temporal visual cortex from pulvinar, claustrum, and amygdala supporting these activations (Grimaldi et al., 2016).
evidence: Inference from activation pattern with cited anatomical pathways.

claim: Given that the day-to-day behaviour of monkey S did not cause concern, the monkey presumably had a reasonable amount of residual vision, in spite of the extensive cortical lesions.
source: Given that the day-to-day behaviour of monkey S did not cause concern, the monkey presumably had a reasonable amount of residual vision, in spite of the extensive cortical lesions.
evidence: Inference from behavioral observations.

claim: It appears that the dorsal visual network was intact in monkey S, and would have the potential to support active vision.
source: Considering all the evidence, it appears that the dorsal visual network was intact, and would have the potential to support active vision (Koyama et al., 2004; Davare et al., 2011), as seen in a number of human patients with damage to the visual cortical system (Goodale and Milner, 1992; Bridge et al., 2013; Goodale, 2011).
evidence: Inference from imaging data with cited parallels to human cases.

claim: Retinal information may reach the dorsal visual areas via the weak pathways with LGN and pulvinar in monkey S.
source: Retinal information may reach the dorsal visual areas via the weak pathways with LGN and pulvinar, but the lack of consistent visual cortex activation, possibly due to the anaesthesia, makes this question difficult to answer.
evidence: Speculation about visual pathways with acknowledgment of uncertainty.

claim: The lack of significant differences between monkey S and controls in the pathways between LGN-V5/MT and pulvinar-V5/MT suggests either or both could support residual visual abilities.
source: The lack of significant differences between monkey S and controls in the pathways between LGN-V5/MT and pulvinar-V5/MT suggests either or both could support residual visual abilities.
evidence: Inference from comparative tractography data.

claim: One possibility for the source of visual input supporting visual function in monkey S could be some preserved V1 connectivity.
source: So, what might be the source of visual input that supports visual function and presumably shaped an intact extrastriate visual brain network? One possibility could be some preserved V1 connectivity.
evidence: Speculation about potential mechanisms.

claim: Given the size and location of the bilateral lesion, the argument for preserved V1 connectivity is difficult to sustain.
source: But given the size and location of the bilateral lesion, this argument is difficult to sustain.
evidence: Inference from lesion characteristics.

claim: Another possibility for visual input would be parallel, alternative inputs to cortex.
source: Another possibility would parallel, alternative inputs to cortex.
evidence: Speculation about alternative mechanisms.

claim: Earlier MRI studies in V1-lesioned monkeys have shown parallel activation in early visual areas, like V2, V3 and V4 as well as V5/MT.
source: Earlier MRI studies in V1-lesioned monkeys have shown parallel activation in early visual areas, like V2, V3 and V4 as well as V5/MT (Schmid et al., 2010).
evidence: Cited findings from previous monkey studies.

claim: It has been suggested that V2 might be a crucial contribution to visual function and awareness.
source: It has been suggested that V2 might be a crucial contribution to visual function and awareness (Merigan et al., 1993).
evidence: Cited hypothesis from literature.

claim: Visual cortical areas V2, V3, and V4 also receive direct subcortical input.
source: These visual cortical areas also receive direct subcortical input (Wong-Riley, 1976; Kaas and Lyon, 2007).
evidence: Cited anatomical findings.

claim: Based on knowledge of functional representations, the activation of face patches in temporal cortex must be driven by a visual subcortical input other than to V5/MT.
source: Based on our knowledge of functional representations, the activation of face patches in temporal cortex discussed above must be driven by a visual subcortical input other than to V5/MT.
evidence: Inference from functional specialization and activation patterns.

claim: It is likely to be a wider pattern of cortical activation that underpins visual awareness and behaviour.
source: Since it is likely to be a wider pattern of cortical activation that underpins visual awareness and behaviour (e.g. Papanikolaou et al., 2019), it might be supported by a wider pattern of weak, parallel subcortical inputs directly to extrastriate visual cortex.
evidence: Cited theoretical framework with inference.

claim: Visual awareness and behaviour might be supported by a wider pattern of weak, parallel subcortical inputs directly to extrastriate visual cortex.
source: Since it is likely to be a wider pattern of cortical activation that underpins visual awareness and behaviour (e.g. Papanikolaou et al., 2019), it might be supported by a wider pattern of weak, parallel subcortical inputs directly to extrastriate visual cortex.
evidence: Speculation based on cited framework and current findings.

claim: Visual structures, both cortical and subcortical, outside of the large lesion of primary visual cortex remained intact in monkey S with little evidence of atrophy.
source: Visual structures, both cortical and subcortical, outside of the large lesion of primary visual cortex remained intact in monkey S with little evidence of atrophy.
evidence: Summary of structural imaging findings.

claim: The intact visual structures in monkey S suggest a role in residual visual function, consistent with an intact network of extrastriate cortical visual areas that was comparable to control monkeys.
source: This suggests a role in residual visual function, consistent with an intact network of extrastriate cortical visual areas that was comparable to control monkeys.
evidence: Inference from structural and functional connectivity findings.

claim: While the structural connectivity between the subcortical regions and area V5/MT was weak in monkey S, the microstructure was intact.
source: While the structural connectivity between the subcortical regions and area V5/MT was weak, the microstructure was intact.
evidence: Summary of tractography findings.

claim: Unlike adult-acquired lesions, there appeared to be a maintenance of structural integrity of the visual system when V1 is damaged neonatally.
source: Thus, unlike adult-acquired lesions, there appeared to be a maintenance of structural integrity of the visual system when V1 is damaged neonatally.
evidence: Inference from comparison with adult-acquired lesion literature.

claim: The maintenance of structural integrity may explain the increased residual function both in monkey S and in children with early damage to the visual cortex.
source: This may explain the increased residual function both, in monkey S and in children with early damage to the visual cortex.
evidence: Inference connecting findings to functional outcomes.

claim: Primary visual cortex (V1) of primates is the major gateway for feedforward input of visual information from the retina via the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) into a network of over 30 extrastriate visual areas.
source: Primary visual cortex (V1) of primates is the major gateway for feedforward input of visual information from the retina via the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) into a network of over 30 extrastriate visual areas (Felleman and Van Essen, 1991; Markov et al., 2014; Schmidt et al., 2018).
evidence: Established anatomical knowledge with citations.

claim: V1 contains a complete, high resolution retinotopic map.
source: V1 contains a complete, high resolution retinotopic map and contributes to cortical processing by computing local spatio-temporal correlations of the input, which is evident in its neural representations of local visual features (orientation, spatial frequency, temporal frequency, direction, colour, binocular disparity) (e.g. Hubel and Wiesel, 1959; Movshon et al., 1978; Parker et al., 2016).
evidence: Established neurophysiological knowledge with citations.

claim: V1 contributes to cortical processing by computing local spatio-temporal correlations of the input.
source: V1 contains a complete, high resolution retinotopic map and contributes to cortical processing by computing local spatio-temporal correlations of the input, which is evident in its neural representations of local visual features (orientation, spatial frequency, temporal frequency, direction, colour, binocular disparity) (e.g. Hubel and Wiesel, 1959; Movshon et al., 1978; Parker et al., 2016).
evidence: Established neurophysiological knowledge with citations.

claim: The direct contribution of V1 signals to conscious sight is a subject of ongoing scientific debate.
source: The direct contribution of V1 signals to conscious sight is a subject of ongoing scientific debate (e.g. Stoerig, 2006; Ffytche and Zeki, 2011) and is thought to involve feedback as well as feedforward input to V1 (Ress and Heeger, 2003).
evidence: Summary of current scientific debate with citations.

claim: The contribution of V1 to conscious sight is thought to involve feedback as well as feedforward input to V1.
source: The direct contribution of V1 signals to conscious sight is a subject of ongoing scientific debate (e.g. Stoerig, 2006; Ffytche and Zeki, 2011) and is thought to involve feedback as well as feedforward input to V1 (Ress and Heeger, 2003).
evidence: Cited theoretical framework.

claim: Patients with V1 lesions exhibiting residual vision - often without visual awareness - have been termed Blindsight.
source: At the centre of this debate have been patients with V1 lesions exhibiting residual vision - often without visual awareness - a condition termed Blindsight (Riddoch, 1917; Weiskrantz et al., 1974; Cowey, 2010).
evidence: Definition of clinical phenomenon with historical citations.

claim: Previous data on bilaterally cortically blind macaque monkeys suggest that there is a dissociation between use of vision for guiding movement and for awareness and recognition.
source: Previous data on bilaterally cortically blind macaque monkeys suggest that there is a dissociation between use of vision for guiding movement and for awareness and recognition (Leopold, 2012).
evidence: Cited findings from monkey studies.

claim: Monkey Helen, who had V1 removed bilaterally, was able to navigate around the world but unable to recognise faces or food.
source: Specifically, monkey Helen, who had V1 removed bilaterally, was able to navigate around the world but unable to recognise faces or food (Humphrey, 1974).
evidence: Cited case study from monkey literature.

claim: The lesions to Helen were made in adulthood, which may have affected the amount of residual vision.
source: The lesions to Helen were made in adulthood, which may have affected the amount of residual vision.
evidence: Inference about timing effects on outcomes.

claim: Macaque monkeys who received a unilateral V1 lesion at two months of age exhibited more residual vision as adults than monkeys who received their lesions in adulthood.
source: Macaque monkeys who received a unilateral V1 lesion at two months of age exhibited more residual vision as adults than monkeys who received their lesions in adulthood (Moore et al., 1996).
evidence: Cited experimental findings showing age-dependent effects.

claim: Cortical blindness due to bilateral damage to the primary visual cortex of humans is fortunately rare.
source: Cortical blindness due to bilateral damage to the primary visual cortex of humans is fortunately rare.
evidence: Statement about clinical epidemiology.

claim: There are a few cases of adult-acquired bilateral V1 damage, some of whom have been extensively studied.
source: There are a few cases of damage acquired in adulthood, some of whom have been extensively studied (de Gelder et al., 2008; Hervais-Adelman et al., 2015; Arcaro et al., 2018), but also a number of children who acquired lesions congenitally or through perinatal stroke (Mundinano et al., 2017).
evidence: Summary of case literature with citations.

claim: There are a number of children who acquired V1 lesions congenitally or through perinatal stroke.
source: There are a few cases of damage acquired in adulthood, some of whom have been extensively studied (de Gelder et al., 2008; Hervais-Adelman et al., 2015; Arcaro et al., 2018), but also a number of children who acquired lesions congenitally or through perinatal stroke (Mundinano et al., 2017).
evidence: Summary of case literature with citation.

claim: The presence of residual visual function suggests that functional visual networks can develop or be sustained in the absence of the main visual input to cortex.
source: The presence of residual visual function suggests that functional visual networks can develop or be sustained in the absence of the main visual input to cortex.
evidence: Inference from clinical observations.

claim: In monkeys, in the absence of primary visual cortex, direct input to extrastriate visual cortex bypassing V1 may arise from the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) or the pulvinar nucleus directly to extrastriate visual areas V2, V3, V4, V5/MT and inferotemporal cortex.
source: In monkeys, in the absence of primary visual cortex, a number of potential pathways have been proposed to convey visual information from the eyes to extrastriate visual cortex. Direct input to extrastriate visual cortex bypassing V1 may arise from the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) or the pulvinar nucleus directly to extrastriate visual areas V2, V3, V4, V5/MT and inferotemporal cortex (Wong-Riley, 1976; Sincich et al., 2004; Kaas and Lyon, 2007; Warner et al., 2010; Gattass et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited anatomical pathways from monkey studies.

claim: In humans, both pulvinar and LGN inputs to V5/MT have been implicated in residual vision.
source: In humans, both pulvinar and LGN inputs to V5/MT have been implicated (de Gelder et al., 2008; Ajina et al., 2015b).
evidence: Cited findings from human studies.

claim: The LGN receives projections from the superior colliculus (SC) in addition to its direct retinal input.
source: In addition to its direct retinal input, the LGN also receives projections from the superior colliculus (SC) (Harting et al., 1991; Stepniewska et al., 1999).
evidence: Cited anatomical findings.

claim: The pulvinar nucleus receives input from the SC, although likely not into the appropriate subdivision for projections to V5/MT.
source: The pulvinar nucleus receives input from the SC, although likely not into the appropriate subdivision for projectiions to V5/MT, and pulvinar might receive surviving early projections directly from the retina (Stepniewska et al., 1999; Warner et al., 2010).
evidence: Cited anatomical findings with qualification.

claim: Pulvinar might receive surviving early projections directly from the retina.
source: The pulvinar nucleus receives input from the SC, although likely not into the appropriate subdivision for projectiions to V5/MT, and pulvinar might receive surviving early projections directly from the retina (Stepniewska et al., 1999; Warner et al., 2010).
evidence: Cited anatomical possibility.

claim: It has been suggested that early-life V1 lesions in particular might lead to less pruning of the retina-pulvinar-V5/MT pathway and that this might contribute to 'blindsight'.
source: It has been suggested that early-life V1 lesions in particular might lead to less pruning of the retina-pulvinar-V5/MT pathway and that this might contribute to 'blindsight' (Warner et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited hypothesis about developmental plasticity.

claim: Macaque monkey S showed bilaterally enlarged lateral ventricles that appeared to have expanded into space usually occupied by V1.
source: Macaque monkey S in the current study showed bilaterally enlarged lateral ventricles that appeared to have expanded into space usually occupied by V1.
evidence: Direct observation from imaging.

claim: The gross pathology of the cerebral cortex in monkey S was most likely to have been acquired developmentally or perinatally.
source: This gross pathology of the cerebral cortex was most likely to have been acquired developmentally or perinatally.
evidence: Clinical inference from imaging characteristics.

claim: Previous data have implicated roles in residual vision for the LGN, pulvinar, SC and the extrastriate visual cortical networks including motion area V5/MT.
source: Previous data have implicated roles in residual vision for the LGN, pulvinar, SC and the extrastriate visual cortical networks including motion area V5/MT.
evidence: Summary of literature on structures supporting residual vision.
